Learning Objectives
Understand the importance of evaluating bone defects before revision total knee arthroplasty.
Understand the Anderson Orthopaedic Research Institute classification of tibial and femoral
defects and how it can help guide surgical management.
Review the concept of zonal fixation in revision total knee arthroplasty.
Epidemiology
Bone loss about a total knee arthroplasty (TKA) implant may be caused by chronic infection,
aseptic loosening, osteolysis, fracture, and stress shielding, or may be caused iatrogenically
during a revision procedure.1

Bone loss about a TKA implant should be evaluated via preoperative imaging studies for
planning purposes and intraoperative imaging to make the final decision regarding implants.
Preoperative physical examination of ligamentous stability
Preoperative imaging
Radiographic imaging: weight-bearing AP/lateral/sunrise views and full-length lower
extremity views to adequately assess bone loss and extremity alignment2 (Resource 1)
Signs of bone loss on radiographs include radiolucent areas around the bone-implant,
bone-cement, or cement-implant interfaces; implant subsidence (especially in the tibial
component); or change in implant position over time.3
Radiolucency around tibial screws in patients with a cementless TKA implant may
indicate screw track osteolysis.4
Defect location around important structures, such as the origin/insertion of the
collateral ligaments or the patellar tendon, is important to consider in evaluating
imaging studies.
Serial imaging studies (if possible) are key to evaluate changes over time.
Plain radiographs tend to underestimate the size of bone defects.
CT may help assess implant positioning/rotation and periprosthetic defects, especially in
patients with osteolysis.3,5,6
Provides more accurate assessment of bone loss than plain radiographs
Intraoperative evaluation
The most accurate method to assess bone loss
Should occur after implant and cement removal and soft-tissue débridement2
After assessment is complete, the decision of how to manage bony defects can be made7
(Resource 2).

Evaluating Bone Defects Before Revision TKA
Preoperative and intraoperative assessments play an important role in the evaluation of
bone defects in patients undergoing revision TKA. Preoperative physical examination of
ligamentous stability will help the surgeon assess whether ligamentous attachments
have been compromised by metaphyseal bone loss and determine the levels of
constraint that should be available during the procedure.1

Preoperative imaging via radiography (and possibly CT) allows the surgeon to make
decisions about the reconstructive materials that should be available during the
procedure, including implant bearing and constraint options, stems, sleeves, cones,
augments, and/or morselized or structural allograft. For example, extensive bone loss
about the tibial or femoral metaphysis (in combination with physical examination
findings of ligamentous laxity) indicates that implants with increased constraint (varus-
valgus constraint and/or rotating-hinge) should be available, whereas bone loss
observed about the tibial tubercle on preoperative imaging necessitates consideration of
options for intraoperative extensor mechanism reconstruction8 (Resource 3).
Finally, intraoperative evaluation after implant removal and debridement provides the
most accurate assessment of bone loss so that real-time reconstructive decisions can be
made.
Anderson Orthopaedic Research Institute Classification
The Anderson Orthopaedic Research Institute (AORI) classification of bone defects is the tool
most used to characterize tibial and femoral defects in patients undergoing revision TKA
(Table 1).
The classification is divided into femoral and tibial metaphyseal bone defects, ranging from
intact (type 1) to damaged (type 2A/B) to deficient (type 3)9 (Resource 4).
Type 2A defects involve damage to one condyle/plateau.
Type 2B defects involve damage to both condyles/plateaus.

General guidelines for the management of bone defects9,10 (Resource 5)
Type 1 defects are contained and may be managed via bone graft or cement.
Type 2A defects (one damaged condyle/plateau) may be managed via augments in the
deficient location and intramedullary stems.
Type 2B defects (damage to both condyles) have predictably greater deficiencies and may
require cones, sleeves, and/or structural allograft with intramedullary stems.
Type 3 defects are the most severe and usually require a tumor-type prosthesis or allograft-
prosthetic composite.

bone defects. A, Type 1, femoral defect. B, Type 1, tibial defect. C, Type 2, femoral defect. D, Type

Anderson Orthopaedic Research Institute Classification
The AORI classification does not strictly dictate the exact surgical management required
but guides the surgeon toward the generally appropriate implant construct. Type 1
defects are the least severe. They may be managed by filling defects smaller than 5 mm
with cement, making sure to drill any particularly sclerotic bone surrounding the defect
to ensure adequate cement interdigitation. Type 1 defects measuring 5 to 10 mm may
be managed via screw-in-cement constructs or augments. Figure 2 shows a screw-in-
cement construct for the management a posteromedial tibial defect during revision TKA.
Cancellous acetabular screws (6.5 mm) are commonly used for this type of construct.11
Figure 2 Intraoperative photograph of a knee shows isolated tibial component revision
for aseptic tibial component loosening with femoral component retention. After the
proximal tibia is prepared for the new tibial component perpendicular to the mechanical
axis, a posteromedial deficiency is managed with the use of two 6.5-mm titanium screws

Type 2 defects often are encountered during revision TKA in patients with aseptic
loosening. Bone loss on only one plateau or condyle is considered a type 2A defect and
can be managed via metal augments to fill the deficient area. Bone loss in both
condyles/plateaus is considered a type 2B defect and requires a larger construct. The
surgeon will need to choose between different combinations of metal augments, cones,
sleeves, or structural allografts depending on preference and/or implant availability.
Many surgeons also will use larger constructs, such as cones/sleeves, in patients with a
type 2A defect for the advantages of long-term biologic fixation.
Type 3 defects can occur in patients who have undergone multiple TKA revision
procedures, with successively greater bone loss after each revision or in patients
undergoing primary TKA who have oncologic bone destruction or a distal femur fracture
in severely osteoporotic bone. These severe defects with deficient metaphyseal bone at
or above the level of the distal femoral epicondyles and/or at or below the level of the
tibial tubercle can be managed via an allograft-prosthetic composite or a
megaprosthesis, reconstructing the entire distal femur/proximal tibia.9,12
Zonal Fixation in Revision TKA13
Zonal fixation refers to the division of the distal femur and proximal tibia into three anatomic
zones of potential fixation (Figure 3): the epiphysis (zone 1), metaphysis (zone 2), and
diaphysis (zone 3).
In revision TKA, the epiphysis, or zone 1, usually is compromised because of the process of
implant failure and/or removal. Therefore, revision will require fixation in zone 2 and/or zone
3, depending on the nature of the defect.
Fixation can be achieved via reconstruction of metaphyseal defects (zone 2) via modular
augmentation (cones, sleeves) versus structural allograft and via stems that may extend to the
diaphysis (zone 3).

This concept of zonal fixation should be used in combination with the AORI classification of
bone defects to help surgeons decide how to reconstruct defects and achieve fixation in
patients undergoing revision TKA and, most importantly, to aid in preoperative planning and
have the necessary implants available during the procedure.
Figure 3 Radiograph demonstrates a failing total knee arthroplasty implant with the fixation
zones identified in planning the revision procedure. (Reproduced with permission from Morgan-
Jones R, Oussedik SIS, Griachen H, Haddad FS: Zonal fixation in revision total knee arthroplasty.
Bone Joint J 2015;97[2]:147-149.)
